questions.stem: The main purpose of civil law is to:
options: set the penalties that apply to drivers who break the road rules in Victoria
protect the rights of individuals, groups and organisations and provide a way to seek redress
punish offenders on behalf of the whole community and deter others from committing similar crimes
maintain social order by allowing the state to prosecute people who break the law
questions.explanation: Civil law protects private rights and allows a wronged party to seek a remedy from the party in breach. Punishing offenders and prosecutions by the state belong to criminal law.

questions.stem: Negligence, defamation, nuisance and trespass are all areas of:
options: criminal law
constitutional law
tort law
contract law
questions.explanation: A tort is a civil wrong that causes harm, and negligence, defamation, nuisance and trespass are all torts. Contract law covers legally binding agreements, which is a separate area of civil law.

questions.stem: A builder stops work on a deck halfway through, in breach of a signed agreement with the home owner. The dispute is best classified as:
options: criminal law
contract law
defamation
nuisance
questions.explanation: The dispute arises from a failure to perform a legally binding agreement, so it is a contract dispute. It is a private matter between the parties, not an offence prosecuted by the state.

questions.stem: A neighbour's workshop releases strong fumes every night that stop Ari from using his backyard. The most relevant area of civil law is:
options: trespass to land
defamation
contract law
nuisance
questions.explanation: Private nuisance is an unreasonable interference with a person's use and enjoyment of their land, such as ongoing fumes or noise. Trespass to land requires a direct physical intrusion onto the land, which drifting fumes are not.

questions.stem: Kim walks across her neighbour's land without permission, causing no damage. Which statement is correct?
options: This is nuisance, because the neighbour's enjoyment was affected
This is negligence, because Kim owed her neighbour a duty of care
This may be trespass to land, even though no damage was caused
This cannot be trespass to land, because no damage was caused
questions.explanation: Trespass to land is an intentional or negligent direct entry onto another's land without permission, and it is actionable without proof of damage. A plaintiff who proves trespass but no loss may receive nominal damages.

questions.stem: In civil law, a breach occurs when:
options: a party refuses to attend a mediation session before trial
a court finds that the defendant is not liable for any loss
a party fails to meet a legal duty or obligation owed to another
a party is charged with a criminal offence by Victoria Police or another body
questions.explanation: A breach is the failure to meet a legal duty or obligation, such as a duty of care or a term of a contract. Being charged by police concerns criminal law.

questions.stem: To establish causation in a civil claim, the plaintiff must show that:
options: the defendant has enough assets to pay any damages awarded
the loss was first reported to the police
the defendant's breach caused the loss suffered
the defendant intended to cause the loss
questions.explanation: Causation links the breach to the loss: the plaintiff must show the loss resulted from the defendant's breach. Intention is not required in many civil claims, such as negligence.

questions.stem: In a civil claim, loss can include:
options: only physical injuries, and never damage to a person's property
only harm that the defendant intended to cause to the plaintiff
both financial losses and non-financial harm such as pain and suffering
only financial losses that can be shown with receipts, invoices or bank records
questions.explanation: Loss includes financial loss, such as medical bills and lost wages, and non-financial harm, such as pain, suffering or damage to reputation. Property damage is also loss, and the harm need not be intended.

questions.stem: A driver negligently clips a cyclist, who suffers only a minor bruise. In hospital, a doctor's grossly negligent treatment then causes the cyclist a serious injury. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The doctor's conduct may be an intervening act that breaks the chain of causation for the serious injury
Neither party can be liable for any of the cyclist's injuries, because the injuries had more than one cause
The doctor cannot be liable, because the driver's negligence is what brought the cyclist into hospital
The cyclist must sue the driver for the treatment, because doctors owe no duty of care to patients
questions.explanation: A later, independent act such as grossly negligent treatment can break the chain of causation, so the driver may not be liable for the serious injury. Doctors owe their patients a duty of care, so the doctor can be liable for the harm the treatment caused.

questions.stem: In civil law, a limitation of actions is:
options: the time limit within which a plaintiff must commence a claim
a cap on the total amount of damages that a court is able to award
a rule limiting the number of witnesses each side may call
the maximum number of days that a civil trial may last
questions.explanation: Limitation of actions laws set the period within which a plaintiff must start legal proceedings. Once the period ends, the claim is generally barred.

questions.stem: Why do limitation periods for civil claims exist?
options: They ensure civil cases are heard after any criminal cases
They give courts enough time to prepare for every trial
Evidence may be lost over time, and defendants deserve certainty
They stop plaintiffs from ever suing government bodies or their employees
questions.explanation: Limitation periods encourage plaintiffs to act promptly, while witnesses' memories and documents are still reliable, and spare defendants the threat of a claim indefinitely. Governments can be sued within the usual limitation periods.

questions.stem: In Victoria, the general limitation period for a defamation claim is:
options: 3 years from the date of discovery
12 years from the date of publication
1 year from the date of publication
6 years from the date of publication
questions.explanation: Defamation has a short limitation period of 1 year from publication, which a court can extend in some circumstances. Six years is the general period for contract and many tort claims.

questions.stem: In Victoria, the general limitation period for a claim for breach of contract is:
options: 6 years from when the cause of action arose
1 year from when the cause of action arose
3 years from when the cause of action arose
12 years from when the cause of action arose
questions.explanation: Under the Limitation of Actions Act 1958 (Vic), contract claims generally must be brought within 6 years of the cause of action arising. One year is the period for defamation.

questions.stem: Cara is injured through negligence but does not realise for some time that her injury was caused by it. For personal injury claims in Victoria, the limitation period is generally:
options: unlimited, because personal injury claims are never subject to a time limit
3 years from when the cause of action is discoverable, subject to a 12-year long-stop
6 years from the date of the negligent act, with no exceptions for later discovery
1 year from the date the injury occurred, with no exceptions for later discovery
questions.explanation: For most personal injury claims, the period is 3 years from when the plaintiff knew or ought to have known the key facts, but no more than 12 years from the act or omission. This protects plaintiffs who discover an injury late while still giving defendants some certainty.

questions.stem: In a civil case, the burden of proof usually rests with:
options: the defendant
the judge
the prosecution
the plaintiff
questions.explanation: The plaintiff brings the claim and so must prove it. There is no prosecution in a civil case.

questions.stem: To meet the standard of proof in a civil case, the plaintiff must show that:
options: their case is more probable than the defendant's
the defendant is liable beyond reasonable doubt
there is only a prima facie case against the defendant
every fact in their claim is proven with certainty
questions.explanation: The civil standard is the balance of probabilities: the plaintiff's version must be more likely than not. Proof beyond reasonable doubt is the higher criminal standard.

questions.stem: A defendant argues that the plaintiff was partly to blame for her own injuries. Who must prove this, and to what standard?
options: The plaintiff, on the balance of probabilities
The plaintiff, beyond reasonable doubt
The defendant, beyond reasonable doubt
The defendant, on the balance of probabilities
questions.explanation: Although the plaintiff bears the burden of proving the claim, a defendant who raises a defence such as contributory negligence must prove it. All civil issues are decided on the balance of probabilities.

questions.stem: A delivery driver negligently injures a pedestrian while making deliveries for his employer. The pedestrian may sue the employer because of:
options: the limitation of actions
vicarious liability
contributory negligence
the doctrine of precedent
questions.explanation: Under vicarious liability, an employer can be liable for wrongs an employee commits in the course of their employment. Contributory negligence concerns the plaintiff's own share of fault.

questions.stem: Why might a plaintiff choose to sue an employer rather than the employee who caused the harm?
options: The employer must prove that it was not negligent once it is sued
Claims against employers are not subject to any limitation period
The employer is more likely to have the money or insurance to pay damages
Employees cannot be sued in civil law for any wrongs they commit while at work
questions.explanation: A plaintiff should consider whether a defendant can actually pay, and employers are more likely to have assets or insurance. Employees can still be sued, and the plaintiff keeps the burden of proof.

questions.stem: A proceeding in which one person sues on behalf of a group of people with similar claims against the same defendant is called a:
options: joint prosecution
committal proceeding
test prosecution
class action
questions.explanation: A class action, also called a representative proceeding, lets a lead plaintiff bring a claim on behalf of a group. It can make it affordable for people with small individual claims to seek a remedy.

questions.stem: In the Supreme Court of Victoria, a class action can be brought only if at least how many people have claims against the same defendant?
questions.explanation: Victoria's class action rules require seven or more people with claims against the same defendant arising out of the same, similar or related circumstances. The claims must also raise a substantial common question of law or fact.

questions.stem: The rights protected by the law of negligence include:
options: the right to be safe from harm caused by another's lack of reasonable care
the right to protect one's reputation from false and damaging public statements
the right to use and enjoy one's land without unreasonable interference
the right to have legally binding agreements honoured by the other party
questions.explanation: Negligence protects people from harm caused by others who fail to take reasonable care. Reputation is protected by defamation, enjoyment of land by nuisance, and agreements by contract law.

questions.stem: Which list sets out the elements of negligence?
options: Duty of care, intention to harm, publication and loss
Offer, acceptance, consideration and intention
Actus reus, mens rea, causation and loss
Duty of care, breach of duty, causation and loss
questions.explanation: To succeed in negligence, the plaintiff must prove the defendant owed a duty of care, breached it, and caused loss as a result. Offer and acceptance are elements of a contract, and actus reus and mens rea belong to criminal law.

questions.stem: In Donoghue v Stevenson (1932), a woman became ill after drinking ginger beer from a bottle that contained a decomposed snail. The court held that:
options: a manufacturer owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer of its product
the café owner was liable for any product it sold on its premises
a person can sue only if they have a contract with the defendant
a consumer must prove the manufacturer intended to cause harm
questions.explanation: The House of Lords held that the manufacturer owed Mrs Donoghue a duty of care even though she had no contract with it, because her friend bought the drink. The case is the foundation of the modern law of negligence.

questions.stem: Lord Atkin's 'neighbour principle' says a duty of care is owed to:
options: only members of the defendant's own family and close friends who live nearby
persons so closely and directly affected that you ought reasonably to have them in mind
everyone who lives in the same street or suburb as the person whose conduct causes the harm
only those people with whom the defendant has entered a legally binding contract
questions.explanation: Lord Atkin said you must take reasonable care to avoid acts you can reasonably foresee would injure your 'neighbour', meaning people closely and directly affected by your conduct. The idea is about foreseeable harm, not where people live or whether there is a contract.

questions.stem: In negligence, a defendant breaches the duty of care if they:
options: do not hold insurance that covers the harm the plaintiff suffered
fail to act as a reasonable person would in the circumstances
fail to prevent every possible harm that could ever occur
intend to cause harm to the plaintiff or the plaintiff's property
questions.explanation: The standard is that of a reasonable person in the defendant's position, not perfection. Negligence does not require intention, and whether the defendant is insured is irrelevant to breach.

questions.stem: A shop employee mops the floor and does not put up a wet-floor sign. A customer slips and breaks her wrist. Which argument best supports a finding of breach of duty?
options: A reasonable shop would have warned customers, as the risk was foreseeable and easy to avoid
The customer was injured, so a breach of the duty of care must have occurred in the shop
The employee did not mean for anyone to slip, so the shop was merely careless rather than at fault
Shops owe no duty of care, because customers enter the premises at their own risk
questions.explanation: Breach is shown by comparing the defendant's conduct with what a reasonable person would have done, considering how foreseeable the risk was and how easily it could have been avoided. An injury alone does not prove a breach.

questions.stem: If a court finds that the plaintiff was partly responsible for their own injury, the usual effect is that:
options: the claim fails completely and the plaintiff receives no damages at all
the defendant must pay extra damages to punish them
the case is transferred to a criminal court for trial
damages are reduced by the plaintiff's share of responsibility
questions.explanation: Contributory negligence is a partial defence: damages are reduced to reflect the plaintiff's share of fault. It does not usually defeat the claim altogether.

questions.stem: Dana accepts a lift from a driver she knows is heavily drunk, and is injured when he crashes. Which defence, if established, would defeat her claim entirely rather than only reduce her damages?
options: Contributory negligence
Honest opinion
Justification
Voluntary assumption of risk
questions.explanation: Voluntary assumption of risk is a complete defence where the plaintiff knew of and freely accepted the risk. Contributory negligence only reduces damages, and honest opinion and justification are defences to defamation.

questions.stem: The usual remedy in a negligence claim is:
options: imprisonment of the defendant
a community correction order
compensatory damages
a fine paid to the state
questions.explanation: Negligence remedies aim to compensate the plaintiff, usually through damages. Fines, imprisonment and community correction orders are criminal sanctions.

questions.stem: Which is an impact of a negligence claim on the defendant who is found liable?
options: The automatic loss of any licence they hold to work in their chosen field
Imprisonment if the damages ordered are not paid within a week
The cost of damages and legal fees, and possible harm to their reputation
A criminal record that is entered as soon as liability is found
questions.explanation: A defendant found liable may face large financial costs and damage to their business or reputation. A civil finding of liability is not a criminal conviction and does not lead to a criminal record.

questions.stem: Defamation law mainly protects:
options: a person's right to speak freely without any limits
a person's physical safety in public places
a person's reputation from unjustified damage
a person's privacy within their home
questions.explanation: Defamation protects people from statements that unjustifiably damage their reputation. It also limits free speech, so it balances reputation against freedom of expression.

questions.stem: Which is an element a plaintiff must establish in a defamation claim?
options: The material was published in a newspaper or broadcast on television
The plaintiff lost money as a direct result of the published material
The material was published to at least one person other than the plaintiff
The defendant intended to harm the plaintiff's reputation by publishing it
questions.explanation: Publication to a third party is required, because reputation is about what others think of the plaintiff. The defendant need not intend harm, and publication can be by any means, including a social media post or a conversation.

questions.stem: A defamatory social media post does not name the plaintiff, but readers can easily tell it refers to her. Can the identification element be satisfied?
options: Yes, if ordinary readers would reasonably identify her from the post
No, because the plaintiff must be named in full somewhere in the material
No, because only printed material can identify a plaintiff
Yes, but only if the post was shared at least 100 times
questions.explanation: A plaintiff is identified if ordinary reasonable people would understand the material refers to them, even without a name. Defamation applies to online material as well as print.

questions.stem: A newspaper reports that a councillor accepted a bribe. The councillor sues for defamation, and the newspaper proves the report is substantially true. The newspaper has established the defence of:
options: justification
honest opinion
qualified privilege
innocent dissemination
questions.explanation: Justification is a complete defence where the defendant proves the imputations are substantially true. Honest opinion protects expressions of opinion, not statements of fact such as accepting a bribe.

questions.stem: A food critic writes that a restaurant's meals are 'bland and overpriced', after describing the meal she ate there. Which defence is most relevant?
options: Absolute privilege
Innocent dissemination
Honest opinion
Justification
questions.explanation: Honest opinion protects an opinion on a matter of public interest that is based on proper material, such as the meal described. 'Bland' is a matter of opinion rather than a fact that can be proven true, which is what justification requires.

questions.stem: During a debate in parliament, a member of parliament makes a defamatory statement about a business owner. Which statement is correct?
options: The business owner can sue if they act within one year
The statement is protected by absolute privilege
The member can be sued because the statement was untrue
The member has a defence of innocent dissemination
questions.explanation: Statements made in parliamentary proceedings are protected by absolute privilege, so no defamation action can succeed, however untrue the statement. The limitation period does not matter if the defence applies.

questions.stem: A newsagent sells a magazine containing a defamatory article. The newsagent did not know about the article and was not negligent in failing to know. The newsagent's best defence is:
options: honest opinion
absolute privilege
innocent dissemination
justification
questions.explanation: Innocent dissemination protects subordinate distributors, such as newsagents and libraries, who did not know and ought not reasonably to have known the material was defamatory. Justification would require the newsagent to prove the article true.

questions.stem: Apart from damages, a plaintiff in a defamation case may seek:
options: an order that the defendant pay a fine
an injunction to stop further publication
an order that the defendant be imprisoned
a community correction order for the defendant
questions.explanation: An injunction can stop a defendant from publishing or continuing to publish defamatory material. Imprisonment, community correction orders and fines are criminal sanctions.

questions.stem: A false post claiming a local builder cheats customers spreads widely online. Which is a likely impact of this breach on the builder?
options: An automatic payment of damages to the builder by the state
Distress and harm to reputation, and possibly lost customers and income
A criminal conviction recorded against the builder for the post
Losing the right to sue anyone else for defamation in the future
questions.explanation: Defamation can cause the plaintiff emotional distress and damage their reputation, which for a business owner may mean lost work and income. The person defamed is not convicted of anything, and any damages must be won from the defendant in a civil claim.
